newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Daewoo Motor to re-enter U.S. car market.
newsitem.headline: Daewoo Motor to re-enter U.S. car market.

text.p: Freed from the constraints imposed by its former partner, South Korea's Daewoo Motor Co said on Tuesday it would re-enter the U.S. market in late 1997 or early 1998 with several new cars.
"We plan to tap the U.S. market again late this year or early next year," said Kim Seung-il, a Daewoo Motor spokesman.
He said Daewoo planned to export 30,000 cars to the world's largest car market in 1998, and 100,000 units in 2000.
Analysts cautioned that Daewoo has a difficult road ahead if it is to achieve its goal.
"The U.S. market is the toughest in the world with fierce competition and low profit margins. Daewoo's move looks risky," said Hur Kang, analyst at Hyundai Securites.
An official at the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association said: "I think Daewoo's chance of success looks to be about 50-50."
Daewoo had agreed to stay out of the U.S. market through 1995 when it ended its partnership with General Motors Corp in late 1992.

During their 15-year partnership, Daewoo and the American car giant were frequently at odds over sales strategy, investment decisions and Daewoo's plans to sell its cars independently in some overseas markets.
Daewoo's LeMans model, based on the West German Opel Kadett, was sold in the U.S. exclusively through GM's Pontiac dealers.
Daewoo launched development of its own models in 1993 after its divorce from GM.
"How our cars will be accepted in the market will set the future of our entire overseas sales," Kim said.
He said Daewoo would set up direct sales outlets in four areas of the U.S.
Models scheduled for export to the U.S. include the Lanos and Nubira compact cars and the Leganza mid-sized sedan.
Daewoo began marketing the Lanos domestically from November 1996, the Nubira from February and the Leganza from April.
The Lanos and Nubira emerged as the country's best sellers in March, and orders for Leganza during first seven days of April have already broken the monthly record for a single model.
"I believe those models are highly competitive in the U.S. market too," said Lee Chang-won, another Daewoo spokesman.
South Korea's vehicle exports to the U.S. hit an all-time high of 481,000 units in 1988, driven by the hugely popular Excel sub-compact model of Hyundai Motor.
The U.S. took more than 80 percent of the nation's total vehicle exports in 1988.
But America's love affair with Korean cars cooled as consumer complaints about quality increased and the yen's fall against the dollar made Japanese cars more competitive.
By 1996, exports to the U.S. had fallen to 201,470 units, only one-sixth of South Korea's total auto exports of 1.2 million units, according to the manufacturers' association.
Daewoo Motor earned 23 billion won ($27.9 million) in net profits last year on sales of 4.3 trillion won. It has targeted profits of 70 billion won in 1997 on sales of 6.8 trillion won.
Kim said Daewoo set a sales target of 885,000 vehicles this year, of which 400,000 units were for export.
In 1996, Daewoo Motor's vehicle sales totalled 653,098 units, including exports of 352,916, he said.
Daewoo has said its production would reach 2.5 million units in 2000, with overseas plants turning out 1.5 million units.
